pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Cumberland, founded 1134 from Furness; its first community driven out by Scots raiders and refounded at Byland)
etymology: From the river Calder, Brittonic caled dwr, hard or violent water, with abbey, Latin abbatia, the house of an abbot.
biblical_def: Calder was settled in 1134 by monks sent from Furness, and within four years a Scottish raid stripped it so thoroughly that the whole community abandoned it and took to the road. Turned away at the mother house, the abbot Gerald and his twelve monks wandered through the north with a single wagon until Gundreda de Gournay gave them the land that became Byland. Calder itself was refounded and lived on as a small, poor house until the dissolution. The episode is the plainest thing the English Cistercians ever did, and it has a text: “they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth” (Heb 11:38). The apostle does not call this failure; he calls it the condition of men “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38). The Psalter knows the same road — “They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in” (Psa 107:4) — and does not leave them on it, for “he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation” (Psa 107:7). A monastery is a walled attempt to have that city now. Calder is the house that was made to learn the opposite, and the lesson is the whole New Testament doctrine of the pilgrim church: “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abbey as a monastery or society of persons secluded from the world and devoted to religion; and wander as to rove, to ramble here and there without any certain course.
webster_full: ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion. The males are called monks, and governed by an abbot; the females are called nuns, and governed by an abbess.
WANDER, v.i. To rove; to ramble here and there without any certain course or object in view.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer; a traveler; particularly, one that travels to a distance from his own country to visit a holy place.
SOJOURN, v.i. To dwell for a time; to dwell or live in a place as a temporary resident.
HABITATION, n. Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling. Place of abode; a settled dwelling; a mansion; a house.
scriptures: (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way; they found no city to dwell in.
And he led them forth by the right way, that they might go to a city of habitation.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
corruption_summary: A house that lost everything to raiders and had to learn on the road what it had been built to teach behind walls.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Calder exposes is not in the raiders but in the settled assumption the raid destroyed — that holiness is a place which can be endowed, walled and kept. Every Cistercian foundation charter is an attempt to buy permanence, and the whole economy of the medieval abbey rested on that attempt. Scripture never grants it. “For here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14) is not consolation offered to the homeless; it is the standing description of the church militant, and twelve men walking north with one wagon were for those months a truer picture of it than the stone they had left.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pilgrim identity of the whole people of God, not of a displaced remnant only. “Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts” (1Pe 2:11) is addressed to settled congregations in Asian cities, not to refugees. The modern form of Calder's mistake is the church that measures its health by its building and its endowment, and is therefore undone by the loss of either.
roots_summary: Latin abbatia, an abbey; Greek planaomai (G4105), to wander; Hebrew taah (H8582), to go astray; Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner; Greek meno (G3306), to abide or continue.
roots_lines: Latin abbatia — an abbey, from abbas, father, from Aramaic abba.
Greek planaomai (G4105) — to wander, to be led astray; “they wandered in deserts” (Heb 11:38).
Hebrew taah (H8582) — to wander, to stray; “They wandered in the wilderness in a solitary way” (Psa 107:4).
Greek parepidemos (G3927) — a resident foreigner, a pilgrim; “as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11).
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain, continue; “here have we no continuing city” (Heb 13:14).
usage: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — said over men with one wagon.
“that they might go to a city of habitation” (Psa 107:7) — the road from Calder to Byland, read theologically.
“but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14) — the sentence a walled abbey is built to forget.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in the Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire, founded 1151 by Roger of Hereford on the spot where his father was killed)
etymology: Old English fleax, flax, and leah, a clearing or meadow — the flax clearing in the forest.
biblical_def: Flaxley was founded in 1151 by Roger, earl of Hereford, on the exact place in the Forest of Dean where his father Milo had been killed by a stray arrow while hunting on Christmas Eve 1143. The abbey was an expiation in stone, raised so that prayer might be made perpetually on the ground where a man had died unprepared. It held forge and iron rights in the forest, grew moderately rich on them, and was dissolved in 1536. The instinct behind the foundation is ancient and not wholly wrong, for blood shed on the ground is never a neutral fact, and the first word Scripture speaks about it is this: “the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10). The law even provided a rite for a death in the open field whose author could not be found, that “the blood shall be forgiven them” (Deu 21:8). But that rite was a confession of guilt, not a purchase of mercy, and it was offered once. What Flaxley attempted was perpetual purchase, and against perpetual purchase stands the single sufficient sacrifice: “For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). An abbey endowed to keep paying for a death long past is the architectural form of unbelief in that sentence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expiation as the act of atoning for a crime, the act of making satisfaction for an offense; and atonement as the expiation of sin made by the obedience and personal sufferings of Christ.
webster_full: EXPIATION, n. The act of atoning for a crime; the act of making satisfaction for an offense, by which the guilt is done away.
ATONEMENT, n. The expiation of sin made by the obedience and personal sufferings of Christ.
BLOOD, n. The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body. Hence, murder; the guilt of murder.
FOREST, n. An extensive wood, or a large tract of land covered with trees.
FLAX, n. A plant of the genus Linum, consisting of a single slender stalk, the skin or herl of which is used for making thread and cloth.
scriptures: Gen 4:10
And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground.
Deu 21:8
Be merciful, O LORD, unto thy people Israel, whom thou hast redeemed, and lay not innocent blood unto thy people of Israel's charge. And the blood shall be forgiven them.
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
Heb 9:26
For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
corruption_summary: An abbey raised on the spot where a man died, to keep paying for a death that one offering had already answered.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the chantry instinct in its purest form: an endowment that buys an unending stream of masses because the one offering is not believed to be enough. Flaxley is unusually honest about it, since the site itself is the argument. Hebrews answers the whole economy at a stroke: “but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Heb 9:26). The word is once, and a house founded to repeat what was done once stands against its own gospel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the finality of the cross against every scheme of instalment payment for guilt. The modern instalments are not masses; they are the endless self-reproach and the commemorative project that can never be finished because it is not believed to be finishable. “he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified” (Heb 10:14) ends both.
roots_summary: Old English fleax leah, flax clearing; Hebrew dam (H1818), blood; Hebrew kaphar (H3722), to cover or make atonement; Greek hapax (G530), once for all; Greek teleioo (G5048), to perfect.
roots_lines: Old English fleax + leah — the flax clearing in the forest.
Hebrew dam (H1818) — blood; “the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me” (Gen 4:10).
Hebrew kaphar (H3722) — to cover, to make atonement; “And the blood shall be forgiven them” (Deu 21:8).
Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; “but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared” (Heb 9:26).
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to complete, to perfect; “he hath perfected for ever” (Heb 10:14).
usage: “crieth unto me from the ground” (Gen 4:10) — why men build on the spot.
“to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Heb 9:26) — why they need not.
“For by one offering” (Heb 10:14) — the sentence that dissolves a chantry.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Essex, founded 1153 as a daughter of Warden; its gate chapel survives as a parish church)
etymology: Old English tilte, probably tilled or cultivated land, with the common Essex place-name ending — the cultivated holding.
biblical_def: Tilty was founded in 1153 by Maurice FitzGeoffrey, a daughter of Warden in Bedfordshire and therefore of Rievaulx's line. It was never large, but it is remembered for an act of shelter: in 1238 it took in the countess of Essex and her children while her husband stood in the king's disfavour, and it did so knowing the cost. The abbey's outer gate chapel outlived the house and still serves as the parish church. A monastery that opens its gate to the hunted is doing something the law of Moses had already built into the land, for Israel was commanded to “appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither” (Num 35:11). Those cities were not a loophole for the guilty but a defence of the unconvicted against private vengeance. Behind them stands the thing they picture: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1), and “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). The prophet makes shelter the measure of a true man — “a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest” (Isa 32:2) — which is the standard Tilty met once, and the standard by which every house that refuses the fugitive is judged.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refuge as shelter or protection from danger or distress, and a place that gives it; and covert as a shelter, a defense, a thing that conceals.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress. That which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity; a strong hold which protects by its strength, or a sanctuary which secures safety by its sacredness.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple. Hence, a place of protection; a sacred asylum.
COVERT, n. A shelter; a defense. A thicket; a hiding place.
ASYLUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors shelter themselves from justice.
SHELTER, n. That which covers or defends from injury or annoyance; a protection.
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
Psa 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Isa 32:2
And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land.
corruption_summary: A small abbey remembered for opening its gate to a family in disgrace, and for the chapel that outlived the house.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption near this entry is the medieval right of sanctuary as it actually worked — a legal immunity that, detached from the cities of refuge and their elders' inquest, sheltered the plainly guilty from the magistrate God had armed. Scripture gives the magistrate the sword and gives the innocent the gate, and will not let either swallow the other. Tilty's act was the good form: shelter for a family not convicted of anything, at risk to itself.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that shelter is a duty with a cost, not a posture. “as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land” (Isa 32:2) describes a man, not an institution, and the institution is only ever as good as the men in it who are willing to be inconvenienced. A church that offers refuge only when refuge is cheap has not offered it.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqlat (H4733), a refuge or asylum; Hebrew machaseh (H4268), a shelter; Hebrew migdal (H4026), a tower; Hebrew cether (H5643), a covering or hiding place; Greek kataphuge, a place of flight.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge, an asylum; “cities of refuge for you” (Num 35:11).
Hebrew machaseh (H4268) — a shelter, a refuge; “God is our refuge and strength” (Psa 46:1).
Hebrew migdal (H4026) — a tower; “The name of the LORD is a strong tower” (Pro 18:10).
Hebrew cether (H5643) — a covering, a hiding place; “as an hiding place from the wind” (Isa 32:2).
Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow; “as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land” (Isa 32:2).
usage: “that the slayer may flee thither” (Num 35:11) — the law's own gate.
“the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10) — the thing the cities pictured.
“a covert from the tempest” (Isa 32:2) — the measure of a man, not a building.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Essex, founded 1140 by King Stephen and Queen Matilda; home of the chronicler Ralph of Coggeshall and of the earliest post-Roman English brickwork)
etymology: Old English personal name Cogg with halh, a nook or corner of land — Cogg's nook.
biblical_def: Coggeshall was founded in 1140 by King Stephen and Queen Matilda, first as a Savigniac house and Cistercian from 1147. Two things make it worth an entry. Its abbot Ralph of Coggeshall wrote the Chronicon Anglicanum, one of the sharpest English chronicles of the thirteenth century, and its buildings carry the earliest medieval brickwork in England, kilned on site when brick had not been made in the island since the legions left. Both are biblical subjects. Brick enters Scripture twice and badly: once at Babel, where men said “Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly” (Gen 11:3) and built to reach heaven, and once in Egypt, where Israel's lives were made bitter “in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field” (Exo 1:14). Brick is the material of human self-assertion and of forced labour, and the Cistercians made it to build a house of prayer, which is either a redemption of the material or a warning. The chronicle is the better of the two, for God himself keeps one: “a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD” (Mal 3:16), and “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines brick as a mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine, then formed into a long square and burnt; and chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time.
webster_full: BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine by grinding or treading, then formed into a long square and burnt in a kiln.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time. It is nearly synonymous with annals.
MORTAR, n. A mixture of lime and sand with water, used as a cement for uniting stones and bricks in walls.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing which had been formed by a previous impression.
RECORD, v.t. To register; to enroll; to write or enter in a book or on parchment, for the purpose of preserving authentic evidence of a fact.
scriptures: Gen 11:3
And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter.
Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
Mal 3:16

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name.
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
corruption_summary: A royal abbey that made the first English brick since Rome and kept one of the century's best chronicles — two materials, one honest and one not.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the Babel use of brick, which is not the clay but the sentence that goes with it. “let us make brick, and burn them throughly” (Gen 11:3) is the first recorded industrial process in Scripture, and its purpose was a name and a tower. Any building programme can be made to serve the same end, including a monastic one, and the Cistercians' own statutes against ornament were written precisely because their houses kept drifting toward it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of the written record against both forgetfulness and flattery. Ralph of Coggeshall told the truth about kings who had endowed his house, which is the hard half. God's own book of remembrance is kept “for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name” (Mal 3:16) — a chronicle with no patron to please.
roots_summary: Hebrew lebenah (H3843), a brick; Hebrew chomer (H2563), clay or mortar; Hebrew zikkaron (H2146), a memorial or record; Hebrew cepher (H5612), a book or writing; Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write.
roots_lines: Hebrew lebenah (H3843) — a brick, from laban, to be white; “let us make brick” (Gen 11:3).
Hebrew chomer (H2563) — clay, mortar; “in morter, and in brick” (Exo 1:14).
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial, a record; “a book of remembrance was written before him” (Mal 3:16).
Hebrew cepher (H5612) — a book, a written document.
Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to inscribe; “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18).
usage: “And they had brick for stone” (Gen 11:3) — the first substitution.
“they made their lives bitter with hard bondage” (Exo 1:14) — what brick cost in Egypt.
“and the LORD hearkened, and heard it” (Mal 3:16) — the chronicle that matters.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Suffolk, founded 1150 by William de Cheney; the only house of the order in that county)
etymology: Old English personal name Sibba with tun, an enclosure or farmstead — Sibba's farm.
biblical_def: Sibton was founded in 1150 by William de Cheney, a daughter of Warden, and it was the only Cistercian abbey in all of Suffolk — one white house in a county thick with black monks and friars. Its cartulary and account rolls survive in unusual fullness and show a middling house that farmed well, lent money, quarrelled with neighbours over sheep, and was surrendered in 1536. The solitary position is the entry's subject. A man who finds himself the only one of his kind in a region is in the oldest spiritual danger there is, and Elijah named it: “I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away” (1Ki 19:14). The answer God gave was not sympathy but a correction of the arithmetic: “Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal” (1Ki 19:18). Solitude distorts the count. The New Testament sets the floor lower than one and the promise higher — “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20) — and the Preacher gives the practical form: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines solitary as living alone, retired, remote from society; and remnant as that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
webster_full: SOLITARY, a. Living alone; not having company. Retired; remote from society.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things.
CORD, n. A string, or small rope, composed of several strands twisted together.
FELLOWSHIP, n. Companionship; society; consort; mutual association of persons on equal and friendly terms.
scriptures: And he said, I have been very jealous for the LORD God of hosts: because the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.
Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Ecc 4:12
And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
corruption_summary: The only white monks in Suffolk, and the oldest temptation of the man who thinks he is the only one left.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the self-pity that masquerades as faithfulness — the conviction, always flattering, that one is the last believer standing. Elijah held it sincerely and was wrong by seven thousand. The posture is corrupt because it quietly makes the remnant the measure of God's work instead of God's work the measure of the remnant, and because a man who believes himself alone stops looking for the brethren he has.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps his count and does not publish it to flatter us. “Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel” (1Ki 19:18) is the sentence for every isolated congregation and every believer in a hostile county. The practical remedy is the ordinary one: find the two or three, because “there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20).
roots_summary: Hebrew badad (H909), to be alone; Hebrew shaar (H7604), to remain or be left over; Greek sunago (G4863), to gather together; Greek mesos (G3319), the midst; Hebrew chut (H2339), a cord or thread.
roots_lines: Hebrew badad (H909) — to be separate, to be alone.
Hebrew shaar (H7604) — to remain, to be left; “I, even I only, am left” (1Ki 19:14).
Hebrew yathar (H3498) — to leave over, to reserve; “Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel” (1Ki 19:18).
Greek sunago (G4863) — to gather together; “where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20).
Hebrew chut (H2339) — a thread, a cord; “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12).
usage: “and they seek my life” (1Ki 19:14) — the complaint God answered with a number.
“all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal” (1Ki 19:18) — the correction.
“two shall withstand him” (Ecc 4:12) — the remedy for one white house in a black county.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Oxfordshire, founded 1147 by Nicholas Basset as a daughter of Waverley)
etymology: Old English bryne, a burning, with aern, a house or place — the burnt place, land cleared by fire.
biblical_def: Bruern was founded in 1147 by Nicholas Basset in the Oxfordshire Cotswolds, a daughter of Waverley and so of the first Cistercian line in England. Its name is the oldest thing about it — ground cleared by fire before any plough touched it. The house was small, chronically in debt, and dissolved in 1536; nothing of the church stands. The name carries the entry. Scripture does not treat fire as mere destruction but as the instrument by which God clears and claims, for “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb 12:29). What fire leaves is ash, and ash is precisely what the gospel exchanges: the Servant is sent “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning” (Isa 61:3), so that the burnt ground is “called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD” (Isa 61:3). The same promise is made to the land itself — “the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1) — and to the man pulled out of the burning, of whom the angel says “is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?” (Zec 3:2). A house named for a burning has the whole doctrine of grace in its deeds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ashes as the earthy particles of combustible substances remaining after combustion; and brand as a burning piece of wood, or a stick or piece of wood partly burnt.
webster_full: ASHES, n. The earthy particles of combustible substances remaining after combustion; as of wood or coal.
BRAND, n. A burning piece of wood; or a stick or piece of wood partly burnt, whether burning or after the fire is extinct.
CONSUME, v.t. To destroy by separating the parts of a thing, by decomposition, as by fire.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
BLOSSOM, n. The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction with their appendages.
scriptures: For our God is a consuming fire.
Isa 61:3

To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
Isa 35:1
The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
Zec 3:2
And the LORD said unto Satan, The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan; even the LORD that hath chosen Jerusalem rebuke thee: is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?
corruption_summary: A poor Cotswold house named for burnt ground, and the exchange Scripture makes on exactly that ground.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption near a name like this is the sentimental reading of fire — the modern instinct that treats every burning as senseless loss and God as the consoler who arrives afterward. Scripture has him in the fire, not after it: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb 12:29) stands in the same chapter as the shaking of all things that can be shaken. Comfort that will not say this leaves the sufferer with a God who is sorry but not sovereign.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exchange itself. “beauty for ashes” (Isa 61:3) is not a figure for improved feelings; it is a transaction in which what is given up is real and what is received is better and unearned. The burnt place is not restored to what it was. It is planted with something it could not have grown.
roots_summary: Old English bryne aern, burnt place; Hebrew epher (H665), ashes; Hebrew peer (H6287), a headdress or beauty; Greek pur (G4442), fire; Hebrew ud (H181), a firebrand.
roots_lines: Old English bryne + aern — the burnt place; land cleared by fire.
Greek pur (G4442) — fire; “our God is a consuming fire” (Heb 12:29).
Hebrew epher (H665) — ashes; “beauty for ashes” (Isa 61:3).
Hebrew ud (H181) — a firebrand, a stick snatched from the fire; “a brand plucked out of the fire” (Zec 3:2).
Hebrew arabah (H6160) — a desert plain; “the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose” (Isa 35:1).
usage: “the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness” (Isa 61:3) — the exchange, stated in full.
“The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan” (Zec 3:2) — said over a man still smoking.
“The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad” (Isa 35:1) — the burnt ground answered.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Huntingdonshire, founded 1147 by Simon de Senlis; a fen-edge house that drained its own land)
etymology: Old English salt with treow, a tree, or more probably salt-ere, a salter's way — the track by which salt was carried across the fen.
biblical_def: Sawtry was founded in 1147 by Simon de Senlis, earl of Northampton, on the dry edge of the great fen, a daughter of Warden. Its monks cut the Monks' Lode, a channel that drained their land and carried their stone and wool out to Whittlesey Mere, and the house lived by turning marsh into pasture. It was dissolved in 1536 and the church pulled down for materials. Draining a marsh is a biblical image with a sharp edge in it, because the prophet's vision of healed waters makes one exception: when the river from the sanctuary heals the Dead Sea so that “there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither” (Eze 47:9), nevertheless “the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt” (Eze 47:11). Some ground is reserved for salt and is not meant to be reclaimed. The promise to the parched is unambiguous — “the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water” (Isa 35:7) — but the marsh stands for what cannot live without mire, and Job asks the question that settles it: “Can the rush grow up without mire?” (Job 8:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines marsh as a tract of low land usually or occasionally covered with water; and drain as to filter, to cause to pass off gradually, to empty of liquor by causing it to flow.
webster_full: MARSH, n. A tract of low land, usually or occasionally covered with water, or very wet and miry.
FEN, n. Low land covered wholly or partially with water, but producing sedge, coarse grasses, or other aquatic plants; boggy land; a moor; a marsh.
DRAIN, v.t. To filter; to cause to pass through some porous substance. To empty of liquor by causing it to flow gradually.
RUSH, n. A plant of the genus Juncus, growing in wet ground and used for mats and bottoming chairs.
MIRE, n. Deep mud; earth so wet and soft as to yield to the feet.
scriptures: Eze 47:9

And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh.
But the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt.
Isa 35:7
And the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water: in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.
Job 8:11
Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?
corruption_summary: A fen-edge house that lived by draining marsh, and the one tract the prophet says will not be healed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the assumption that every wet place is waste to be reclaimed — the improving instinct that cannot leave a landscape or a soul alone. Ezekiel reserves the marishes to salt, and the reservation is not an oversight. There is ground God keeps for his own purposes, and the drainer who cannot tell improvement from presumption will eventually drain it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is discernment about what is ours to mend. “can the flag grow without water?” (Job 8:11) is Bildad's bad counsel put to good use: some things genuinely die when their element is taken away, and the wise man learns which. The gospel's promise to the parched is unconditional; the promise to the marsh is not.
roots_summary: Hebrew bitstsah (H1207), a marsh or swamp; Hebrew melach (H4417), salt; Hebrew tsimmaon (H6774), thirsty ground; Hebrew gome (H1573), a rush or papyrus; Hebrew raphah (H7495), to heal.
roots_lines: Hebrew bitstsah (H1207) — a swamp, a marsh; “the marishes thereof shall not be healed” (Eze 47:11).
Hebrew melach (H4417) — salt; “they shall be given to salt” (Eze 47:11).
Hebrew raphah (H7495) — to heal, to mend; “for they shall be healed” (Eze 47:9).
Hebrew tsimmaon (H6774) — parched ground, thirsty land; “the thirsty land springs of water” (Isa 35:7).
Hebrew gome (H1573) — a rush, papyrus; “Can the rush grow up without mire?” (Job 8:11).
usage: “every thing shall live whither the river cometh” (Eze 47:9) — the general promise.
“shall not be healed” (Eze 47:11) — the exception the drainers forget.
“in the habitation of dragons, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes” (Isa 35:7) — the fen, read forward.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Lincolnshire, founded 1139 by Bishop Alexander of Lincoln; its chronicle gives a notable English account of the Black Death)
etymology: From the town of Louth, Old English from the river Lud, with park, an enclosed tract of ground — the abbey in the bishop's park at Louth.
biblical_def: Louth Park was founded in 1139 by Alexander, bishop of Lincoln, as a daughter of Fountains, and sat in an enclosed park outside the town. Its lasting value is a book: the Chronicon Abbatiae de Parco Lude, which records, among much else, the coming of the pestilence in 1349 with a plainness most chroniclers could not manage — the dead uncounted, the fields unploughed, the abbey itself emptied. The abbot died of it. Scripture does not treat pestilence as a riddle. It names it, assigns it, and refuses both of the comfortable readings: that it means nothing, and that it falls only on the worse. “I have sent among you the pestilence after the manner of Egypt” (Amo 4:10) is followed by the burden of the whole passage, “yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amo 4:10) — the judgement is that it taught nothing. The believer's confidence is not exemption but covering: “Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday” (Psa 91:6). And the right use of a plague year is the Psalmist's: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pestilence as plague, appropriately so called, and any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal; and number as to count, to reckon, to ascertain the units of any sum.
webster_full: PESTILENCE, n. Plague, appropriately so called; but in a general sense, any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.
PLAGUE, n. Any thing troublesome or vexatious; but appropriately, a malignant contagious fever, that often prevails in Egypt, Syria and Turkey.
NUMBER, v.t. To count; to reckon; to ascertain the units of any sum, collection or multitude.
CHRONICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying. Frequency of death; actual death of great numbers of men or beasts.
scriptures: Amo 4:10

I have sent among you the pestilence after the manner of Egypt: your young men have I slain with the sword, and have taken away your horses; and I have made the stink of your camps to come up unto your nostrils: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
Psa 91:6
Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
And he stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed.
corruption_summary: A Lincolnshire house whose chronicle told the truth about the plague year, including about itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the two false readings of a plague, and the fourteenth century produced both. One made the pestilence a verdict on the neighbours, and sent flagellants and mobs through Europe. The other made it meaningless, and sent men to the tavern. Amos cuts across both: the pestilence is sent, and the sin it exposes is not the victims' particular wickedness but the survivors' failure to return. “yet have ye not returned unto me” (Amo 4:10) is the indictment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Moses' arithmetic. “So teach us to number our days” (Psa 90:12) is the only numbering a plague year genuinely demands, and it is a prayer, not a resolution. Aaron's posture in the camp is the other half, for he “stood between the dead and the living; and the plague was stayed” (Num 16:48) — a picture of priestly intercession that no chronicle can replace.
roots_summary: Hebrew deber (H1698), pestilence; Hebrew maggephah (H4046), a plague or blow; Hebrew manah (H4487), to number or appoint; Hebrew shuwb (H7725), to return or repent; Greek loimos, a pestilence.
roots_lines: Hebrew deber (H1698) — pestilence; “the pestilence that walketh in darkness” (Psa 91:6).
Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — a plague, a blow; “and the plague was stayed” (Num 16:48).
Hebrew shuwb (H7725) — to turn back, to return; “yet have ye not returned unto me” (Amo 4:10).
Hebrew manah (H4487) — to count, to number, to appoint; “So teach us to number our days” (Psa 90:12).
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, skill; “that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12).
usage: “after the manner of Egypt” (Amo 4:10) — the plague named, not explained away.
“the destruction that wasteth at noonday” (Psa 91:6) — covering, not exemption.
“between the dead and the living” (Num 16:48) — where the priest stands.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Lincolnshire, founded 1148; the house of the legend that a monk poisoned King John)
etymology: Old English swin, swine, with heafod, a headland or promontory — the swine's headland, a spur of dry ground in the fen.
biblical_def: Swineshead was founded in 1148 by Robert de Gresley, a Savigniac house that became Cistercian in 1147 with the rest of that congregation. It is remembered almost entirely for something that did not happen. King John stopped there in October 1216, a few days after losing his baggage train in the Wash, and died shortly afterward at Newark of dysentery. Within a generation the story had hardened into a monk of Swineshead poisoning him in a cup of ale, and Shakespeare put it on the stage. No contemporary who was near the king says any such thing. The abbey therefore stands under a text it did not choose: “Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness” (Exo 23:1). The ninth commandment is not a rule about courtroom perjury only; it governs the story a man repeats because it is satisfying. “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16) covers the dead as well as the living, and Proverbs supplies the discipline that would have killed the legend in a week: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slander as a false tale or report maliciously uttered, tending to injure the reputation of another; and report as an account returned, a story or relation circulated.
webster_full: SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another by lessening him in the esteem of his fellow citizens.
REPORT, n. An account returned; a statement or relation of facts given in reply to inquiry. Rumor; story circulated.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. That which furnishes evidence or proof.
CALUMNY, n. Slander; false accusation of a crime or offense, knowingly or maliciously made or reported, to the injury of another.
POISON, n. Any substance which, when taken into the stomach, mixed with the blood, or applied to the skin, is capable of destroying life.
scriptures: Exo 23:1
Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Pro 14:5
A faithful witness will not lie: but a false witness will utter lies.
corruption_summary: A fen abbey known for a murder it did not commit, and the ninth commandment as it governs a good story.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the satisfying lie, which needs no malice to spread — only an audience that wants it true. The Swineshead legend grew because John was hated and a poisoning monk made a better ending than dysentery at Newark. Scripture puts the burden on the repeater, not merely the inventor: “put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness” (Exo 23:1) makes the man who passes the tale a party to it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ninth commandment binds the hearer. “but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17) is a rule of method: no account is settled until the other side has been heard, and a man who is dead cannot answer. The modern engine for this is faster than a chronicle and has the same defect, which is that a story that flatters our judgement is never examined.
roots_summary: Hebrew shav (H7723), falsehood or emptiness; Hebrew ed (H5707), a witness; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), a lie or deception; Hebrew rea (H7453), a neighbour; Hebrew chaqar (H2713), to search out.
roots_lines: Hebrew shav (H7723) — emptiness, falsehood; “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exo 23:1).
Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; “A faithful witness will not lie” (Pro 14:5).
Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — a lie, deception; “but a false witness will utter lies” (Pro 14:5).
Hebrew rea (H7453) — a neighbour, an associate; “false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16).
Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, to examine; “his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17).
usage: “Thou shalt not raise a false report” (Exo 23:1) — the commandment the legend broke.
“He that is first in his own cause seemeth just” (Pro 18:17) — why the first telling won.
“A faithful witness will not lie” (Pro 14:5) — the standard for a chronicler.

pos: n. (a Cistercian abbey in Holderness, Yorkshire, founded 1151 by William le Gros in commutation of a crusading vow)
etymology: From the Norman place-name Meaux in Brie, carried to Holderness by its founder's men, with abbey, Latin abbatia.
biblical_def: Meaux was founded in 1151 by William le Gros, count of Aumale and lord of Holderness, a daughter of Fountains. The abbey's own chronicler, Thomas Burton, writing two centuries later, gives the reason without flinching: the count had vowed to go on crusade, found himself too old and too heavy to go, and obtained from the pope a commutation of the vow into the founding of a monastery. Burton's Chronica Monasterii de Melsa is one of the fullest house histories in England, and it is honest about its own origin. That origin is the entry's subject. Scripture treats a vow as a debt that the mouth has created and the hand must pay: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecc 5:4), and the law is blunter still, for “the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee” (Deu 23:21). The Preacher's remedy is not a cheaper substitute but silence beforehand: “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5). And the man God welcomes is the one “that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vow as a solemn promise made to God, and commute as to exchange, to put one thing in the place of another, to give or receive one thing for another.
webster_full: VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity. A vow is a promise of something to be given or done hereafter.
COMMUTE, v.t. To exchange; to put one thing in the place of another; to give or receive one thing for another.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.
CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land from the infidels.
PAY, v.t. To discharge a debt; to deliver to a creditor the value of a debt, either in money or goods.
scriptures: Ecc 5:4
When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.
Ecc 5:5
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
corruption_summary: An abbey founded because its patron could not keep the vow he had made, and bought a substitute for it instead.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is commutation itself — the machinery by which a vow made to God became a transaction negotiable with a church office. Once a vow can be exchanged for a payment, the vow has stopped being a vow and become an opening bid. Meaux is a beautiful building raised on that principle, and its own chronicler says so. “he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4) is the Preacher's verdict on the man who speaks faster than he can pay.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the remedy for a rash vow is not a discount but repentance and, where possible, performance. “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow” (Ecc 5:5) is counsel for the future, not absolution for the past. The modern commutation is the pledge quietly downgraded, the promise to a spouse or a congregation renegotiated on grounds of difficulty — and “He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4) remains the description of the man who may dwell in God's hill.
roots_summary: Hebrew neder (H5088), a vow; Hebrew shalam (H7999), to complete or pay; Hebrew darash (H1875), to require or seek; Hebrew shaba (H7650), to swear; Hebrew machar (H4171), to exchange.
roots_lines: Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, a votive offering; “When thou vowest a vow unto God” (Ecc 5:4).
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to complete, to make good, to pay; “pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecc 5:4).
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to require; “will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21).
Hebrew shaba (H7650) — to swear, to bind oneself by oath; “He that sweareth to his own hurt” (Psa 15:4).
Hebrew machar (H4171) — to change, to exchange — the root idea behind commutation.
usage: “defer not to pay it” (Ecc 5:4) — the law a commutation evades.
“and it would be sin in thee” (Deu 23:21) — the cost of not paying.
“and changeth not” (Psa 15:4) — the man who does not need a dispensation.
